blocks.text: Imagine running multiple tasks simultaneously on your computer, like editing a document while listening to music. How does your operating system manage these tasks efficiently?

blocks.markdown: In modern operating systems, threads are a fundamental concept that allows multiple tasks to be executed concurrently within a single process. Understanding threads is crucial for grasping how operating systems manage multitasking and resource sharing.

blocks.title: Definition of a Thread
blocks.text: A thread is the smallest unit of processing that can be scheduled by an operating system. It is a component of a process that can run independently.

blocks.markdown: Threads are often referred to as 'lightweight processes' because they share the same resources of a process, such as memory and file handles, but can be scheduled to run independently. This allows for efficient execution of tasks that can be performed concurrently.

blocks.title: Key Characteristics of Threads
blocks.text: Threads within the same process share the process's resources, including memory and file descriptors, but each thread has its own stack, program counter, and registers.

blocks.caption: A process can contain multiple threads, denoted as \( T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n \).

blocks.title: Comparing Threads and Processes
blocks.prompt: Consider a process with three threads. What resources are shared among these threads, and what are unique to each thread?

steps.text: Identify the resources shared by threads within a process.
steps.latex: Shared: Memory space, file descriptors, global variables.

steps.text: Identify the resources unique to each thread.

blocks.answer: Threads within a process share memory space, file descriptors, and global variables, but each thread has its own stack, program counter, and registers.

blocks.markdown: Multithreading offers several advantages, such as improved performance through parallelism and better resource utilization. However, it also introduces risks like race conditions and deadlocks.

blocks.title: Risks of Multithreading
blocks.text: Multithreading can lead to complex issues such as race conditions, where threads compete for resources, and deadlocks, where threads wait indefinitely for resources held by each other.

blocks.title: User-Level vs Kernel-Level Threads
blocks.prompt: Explain the difference between user-level and kernel-level threads.

steps.latex: User-level threads are managed by a user-level library and the kernel is unaware of them.
Kernel-level threads are managed directly by the operating system kernel.

blocks.answer: User-level threads are managed by a user-level library and are invisible to the kernel, while kernel-level threads are managed by the operating system kernel itself.

blocks.title: Example of Thread Usage
blocks.text: Web servers often use threads to handle multiple client requests concurrently, allowing for efficient processing and improved response times.

points: Threads are lightweight processes that share resources within a process but have their own execution context.
Multithreading can improve performance but also introduces risks like race conditions and deadlocks.
User-level threads are managed by libraries, while kernel-level threads are managed by the OS kernel.
